title: Bells in Indian (Hindu) temples
sources: General references on Hindu temple worship (puja/aarti practice); no peer-reviewed evidence exists for the health/brain claims

verified.text: Most Hindu temples in India hang a bell (ghanta) near the entrance or in front of the sanctum.
Devotees traditionally ring the bell when they enter the temple, before they pray.
Bells are also rung during aarti and puja, the worship ceremonies.
Temple bells are usually cast from bronze or brass; some are made of panchdhatu, a traditional alloy of five metals.
In tradition, the bell's sound announces the devotee and draws attention away from worldly thoughts toward the deity.

theories.text: It is popularly claimed that the bell's echo lasts about seven seconds and balances the left and right sides of the brain or activates chakras. There is no scientific evidence for this; present it as a belief.
Many people believe the sound drives away negative energy or evil spirits. This is a religious belief, not a scientific finding.

knownErrors.text: Science has proved that temple bells heal the body
knownErrors.correction: No scientific study shows this; it is a belief.

uncertain: Health and brain effects of bell sounds are beliefs; present them with 'it is believed' / 'माना जाता है'.
